title: Number of Distinct Substrings in a String
statement: Count how many different non-empty substrings the string `s` contains and return that count. A substring is a contiguous run of characters, the result of dropping zero or more characters from the front of `s` and zero or more from the back. Substrings are compared as text: two equal pieces taken from different positions count once.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

The direct method puts every substring `s.slice(i, j)` into a set. There are about n²/2 substrings, but each slice costs up to n to build and hash, so that is O(n³). A rolling hash fixes the extra factor: for a fixed start, extending the substring by one character updates its hash in O(1). Equal substrings get equal hashes, so counting distinct hashes counts distinct substrings.

## Approach

1. For every `start`, reset two hashes `hash1` and `hash2` to 0.
2. Move `end` from `start` to the end of `s`. Fold the new character in with `hash = (hash * BASE + code) % MOD`, once for each modulus.
3. Add the pair of hashes, together with the length `end - start + 1`, to the set `seen`.
4. Return `seen.size`.

Two independent moduli make an accidental collision between different substrings extremely unlikely; including the length rules out collisions between substrings of different sizes.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "aabbaba"` has 28 substrings in total. Only four appear more than once: `"a"` (4 times), `"b"` (3 times), `"ab"` (2 times) and `"ba"` (2 times). Each repeat produces the same hash pair and length, so the set keeps one copy. Removing the 3 extra `"a"`, the 2 extra `"b"`, the extra `"ab"` and the extra `"ba"` leaves 28 - 7 = `21`, which is `seen.size`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): each of the n(n+1)/2 substrings is hashed in O(1) from the previous one.
- Space: O(n²) for the set of hashes in the worst case.

## Pitfalls

- Hashing `s.slice(start, end + 1)` from scratch reintroduces the O(n³) cost.
- Keep every product below 2^53: a hash below about 10^9 times `BASE = 131` is safe, but multiplying two hashes together is not.
- A single small modulus can make different substrings collide; use two moduli (or a trie of suffixes, which is exact).
- The empty substring is not counted.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `s` |
| `BASE`, `MOD1`, `MOD2` | polynomial hash base and the two moduli |
| `seen` | set of hash signatures of substrings found so far |
| `start`, `end` | first and last index of the current substring |
| `hash1`, `hash2` | the current substring's hash under each modulus |
| `code` | character code of `s[end]` |

narration.3: Pick a small base for the polynomial hash.
narration.4: Two large primes keep accidental collisions very unlikely.
narration.6: The set will hold one signature per distinct substring.
narration.8: Each start index begins a family of substrings.
narration.9: The empty prefix has hash 0 under both moduli.
narration.11: Extend the substring one character at a time.
narration.13: Shift the old hash one place and fold in the new character.
narration.14: Do the same under the second modulus.
narration.15: Record the substring s[start..end] by its two hashes and its length.
narration.18: The number of distinct signatures is the number of distinct substrings.
